evidence.quote: The park, established in 1958, includes 3,500-acre Kanopolis Lake and a 12,500-acre wildlife area of rolling hills, bluffs and woods

evidence.claim: At the western end, Ellsworth grew as a railroad cattle town in the late 1860s.
evidence.quote: Ellsworth was a bustling cattle town during the late 1860s, when the Kansas Pacific Railroad had a stop and stockyards there.

evidence.claim: Texas herds reached its stockyards for shipment to major markets, but Kansas Pacific closed the pens in 1875 and the trade dwindled.
evidence.quote: Cattle were driven up from Texas to this point, and then shipped to major markets. Often cowboys had the run of the town. In 1875 Kansas Pacific closed its cattle pens, moving to another location. The cattle trade dwindled to almost nothing by the mid-1880s.

evidence.claim: Further along the corridor, a later engineering project changed the Smoky Hill River: the Army Corps of Engineers completed Kanopolis Dam in 1948 for flood control and water conservation.
evidence.quote: Completed in 1948 as a flood control and water conservation project of the United States Army Corps of Engineers, the dam impounds the Smoky Hill River.

evidence.claim: Work had begun in 1940, then stopped in 1942 during World War II. The interruption lasted three and a half years; water storage finally began in February 1948.
evidence.quote: The Flood Control Act of 1938 authorized the construction of Kanopolis Dam and Lake, and the U.S. Army Corps of Engineers began work in June 1940. The outbreak of World War II, however, led to a suspension of the effort in 1942, delaying the project for 3 1/2 years. The Corps of Engineers finally completed construction in 1948 at a cost of $12.3 million. Storage of water in the reservoir began February 17, 1948.

evidence.claim: Start at I-70’s exit 225 and take K-156 into Ellsworth, then K-140 east toward Mushroom Rock.
evidence.quote: Begin on the I-70 exit 225 for K-156 towards Ellsworth KS. Continue on K-156 towards Ellsworth for about 10 miles. Once in Ellsworth, make a left on K-140 for 13 miles towards K-141 near Carneiro, KS. Along the way, be sure to stop by Mushroom Rock State Park .

evidence.claim: K-141 runs south along Kanopolis Lake’s eastern shore and over its dam.
evidence.quote: Kansas Highway 141 runs generally north-south along the reservoir's eastern shore and across the top of Kanopolis Dam.

evidence.claim: Turn east on K-4 toward Lindsborg, then follow Smoky Valley Road to Roxbury and 27th Avenue south to Canton.
evidence.quote: Once you reach the sign for K-4, make a left and head east for 15 miles towards Lindsborg, KS.

evidence.claim: Turn east on K-4 toward Lindsborg, then follow Smoky Valley Road to Roxbury and 27th Avenue south to Canton.
evidence.quote: Stay on Smoky Valley Rd for 13 miles until you reach Roxbury, KS. In Roxbury, turn right onto 27th Ave and drive the final 13 miles to Canton, KS.

evidence.claim: Two mushrooms and a giant shoe give this five-acre park its unusual collection of rock shapes.
evidence.quote: Two mushrooms and a giant shoe rock, as well as numerous other rock formations, are in the 5-acre (2.0 ha) park.

evidence.claim: The formations preserve beach sands and sediments from the Cretaceous Period.
evidence.quote: These rocks are the remains of beach sands and sediments of the Cretaceous Period

evidence.claim: Natural cement holds the sandstone and sedimentary rock together; the mushroom-shaped concretions are cemented with calcium carbonate.
evidence.quote: Sandstone and sedimentary rock are held together by natural cement. The concretions that make up mushroom rocks are cemented calcium carbonate.

evidence.claim: The largest rock measures 27 feet across.
evidence.quote: The largest rock measures 27 feet in diameter.

evidence.claim: This is Kansas’s smallest state park, managed by Kanopolis State Park.
evidence.quote: Mushroom Rock is Kansas's smallest state park

evidence.quote: Two mushrooms and a giant shoe rock

evidence.claim: The Swedish Pavilion traveled to Lindsborg after serving as an exposition building at the 1904 St. Louis World’s Fair.
evidence.quote: the Pavilion was built as an international exposition building for the 1904 Louisiana Purchase Exposition, also known as the St. Louis World's Fair.  After the fair, the Pavilion was moved to Bethany College in Lindsborg, Kansas

evidence.claim: At Bethany College it housed classrooms, a library, a museum and art-department facilities.
evidence.quote: where it was used for classroom, library, museum and department facilities for the art department.

evidence.claim: It moved again in 1969 to the museum now called the Lindsborg Old Mill & Swedish Heritage Museum.
evidence.quote: The Swedish Pavilion was moved to the McPherson County Old Mill Museum, - now the Lindsborg Old Mill & Swedish Heritage Museum - also in Lindsborg, in 1969.

evidence.claim: Immigrants from Sweden’s Värmland province settled Lindsborg in 1869.
evidence.quote: Lindsborg was settled in the spring of 1869 by a group of immigrants from the Värmland province of Sweden

evidence.claim: The town continues to celebrate that heritage through Svensk Hyllningsfest, held every other year.
evidence.quote: Lindsborg has long been noted for the Svensk Hyllningsfest, a biennial celebration

evidence.claim: The pavilion itself remains part of that cultural life: the museum uses it for heritage events on its grounds.
evidence.quote: The facility is used for cultural heritage events at the museum.

evidence.claim: Canton’s two water towers offer a choice their contents do not: one says “HOT” in red, the other “COLD” in blue.
evidence.quote: Canton has two water towers, labeled "HOT" (in red) and "COLD" (in blue).

evidence.claim: Both tanks hold water at ambient temperature.
evidence.quote: In fact, both tanks hold water at an ambient temperature.

evidence.claim: The lettering dates to 1956, when local real estate agent Mrs. M.D. Fisher suggested painting the words as a tourist attraction.
evidence.quote: The words were painted on as a tourist attraction in 1956 at the suggestion of local real estate agent Mrs. M.D. Fisher.

evidence.claim: The tower labels use red for “HOT” and blue for “COLD.”
evidence.quote: Canton has two water towers, labeled "HOT" (in red) and "COLD" (in blue).

flags: Cache does not document construction, campaigning or designation dates for the byway itself; history paragraph instead explains transport and reservoir changes along its corridor.
Official tourism route is 80 miles; material mapped route is 55.8 miles and begins near Terra Cotta. Used the full tourism corridor and kept the shared driving order.
Dropped current “wickedest” characterization: cache offers unattributed historical epithets, not a named source appropriate for the required attribution.
Dropped current claim that pioneers and Native Americans met at Mushroom Rock: cache says it served as a meeting place for both, but does not establish that they met one another or identify nations.

Changed current claim that both Canton tanks hold water at the same temperature to the supported claim that both hold water at ambient temperature. Canton moment stays short because the tower story is complete without unrelated town facts.
Mushroom Rock moment is short because the cache supports a compact geological explanation but does not explain differential erosion or provide a fuller park history.
